title: The 5 Biggest Mistakes in Lesson Observations (aka Learning Walks) And How They Might Drive Teachers Away
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele argues that top-down lesson observation feedback is a hidden driver of teacher stress, burnout and attrition because it undermines psychological safety. He sets out five mistakes, each with the old way, why it fails and a practical fix. Delivering a pre-written monologue should give way to co-constructing the record with the teacher. Judging a teacher from one snapshot, which Robert Coe's work shows is noisy, calls for triangulating evidence over time. Observers who assume causes should inquire before inferring, and asking two students whether they understand is a biased micro-sample better replaced by looking at whole-class work. Finally, unannounced ambushes and hit-and-run debriefs should be replaced by protected reflection time, prompts in advance and equal airtime. He closes by urging leaders to move from an inspection mindset to a coaching one.
points: Observation feedback is a learning process, so the teacher should help write the record rather than receive a finished judgement.
One observed lesson is a snapshot of a snapshot, and development goals should rest on triangulated evidence such as work samples and planning over time.
Observers should ask curious questions about routines and prior learning before assuming an explanation was poor.
Whole-class artefacts such as mini-whiteboard responses and books give better evidence than asking two students if they understand.
Debriefs work best at least a day later, with prompts shared in advance and the teacher speaking for at least half of the meeting.
quotes: Feedback is not a product to be delivered; it is a learning process. When an observer unilaterally drafts the observation document prior to the debrief, they strip the teacher of professional agency.
When feedback is delivered using outdated, top-down approaches, it directly undermines psychological safety and leaves dedicated professionals feeling misjudged, undervalued, and demotivated.
A single lesson is merely a snapshot of a snapshot, a brief window into a complex, multi-month dynamic built on existing routines, long-term schema development, and relational trust.
Assuming intent or root cause without asking the teacher turns feedback into an ungrounded accusation.
Two students out of a class of thirty represent a sample size of under 7%. Making sweeping claims about whole-class learning based on two data points violates basic statistical validity.

Almost no observer sets out with malignant intent. Most leaders inherit feedback systems that were built a decade ago, systems designed around compliance, inspection, and top-down grading rather than cognitive science, deliberate practice, and professional growth.

By shifting from an inspection mindset to a coaching and development mindset, we protect psychological safety, foster genuine teacher growth, and ensure our best educators stay where they belong: in front of the classroom, making a difference.
